passage: The Pune inter-school debate final ended, and the judges called Mridul's name. He grinned so wide his cheeks ached, and punched the air once. Then he went straight to the front row, where Tanuja ma'am was clapping. "Ma'am, you made me rewrite that rebuttal four times. Thank you." On his way out he found Farzana from the other school sitting on the stairs, holding her notes. "Your point on water rights was the best one of the day," he said. "I had no answer to it." She looked up, surprised. On the bus home, his friends wanted him to post the trophy photo everywhere. Mridul shrugged. "Maybe later." He spent the ride on the phone, telling Amma about Farzana's argument.

qa.q: How many times did Tanuja ma'am make Mridul rewrite the rebuttal?
qa.a: She made him rewrite it four times.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when his name was called, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt joyful and proud; he grinned till his cheeks ached and punched the air once.

qa.q: What did Mridul choose to do after winning?
qa.a: He thanked Tanuja ma'am and went to praise Farzana's argument, enjoying his win while staying kind to someone who lost.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt when Mridul praised her point?
qa.a: She likely felt surprised and respected, which could ease the sting of losing.

grounding: A teenager who wins a debate enjoys it, thanks his coach, praises a rival who lost and feels no need to show off.

passage:
"Paati! I won the state 800 metres!"
"Won? Come here, let me see that medal." Lakshmi Paati held it up to the tube light. "Heavy."
"My coach cried. Actually cried. I told him the medal's half his."
"And the boy who came second?"
"Jithin. He fell at the line. I helped him up. He's really good, Paati. Maybe he'll beat me next year."
"You're not going to put it on every chat group?"
Mridul ducked his head, grinning. "Nah. I know I ran well. That's enough."
"Hmm. Then give it here. It goes on the puja shelf."
"Paati! Next to Ganesha?"
"Where else?"

qa.q: Where does Lakshmi Paati want to put the medal?
qa.a: On the puja shelf, next to Ganesha.

qa.q: Why doesn't Mridul want to post the medal on every chat group?
qa.a: He feels secure knowing he ran well, so he doesn't need an audience to feel proud.

qa.q: What choice did Mridul make at the finish line, and what does it show?
qa.a: He helped Jithin up after he fell, showing he could enjoy winning while staying kind to the runner he beat.

qa.q: How might Mridul's coach feel hearing the medal is half his?
qa.a: He probably feels moved and valued, which fits with him crying.

grounding: A teenager enjoys a state win, credits his coach, is kind to the runner-up and needs no audience for his pride.

passage:
Friday: Nandini stayed after practice to thank Coach Hafsa for the drills on her backhand. "Don't thank me yet," Hafsa laughed.
Saturday, the final: Nandini won the district badminton title against Kiran, a girl she'd lost to twice before. She jumped and yelled, then walked straight to the net to shake Kiran's hand. "Your smashes were brutal. I got lucky on that last rally."
Monday: At school, a boy said, "You crushed that loser." Nandini frowned. "She's not a loser. She nearly beat me." She didn't post the trophy photo. It sat on her desk, where she could see it while studying.

qa.q: Who did Nandini beat in the final?
qa.a: Kiran, a girl she'd lost to twice before.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when she won?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, jumping and yelling, and still grateful and respectful towards Kiran.

qa.q: What did Nandini do on Monday that showed pride without contempt?
qa.a: She refused to call Kiran a loser and pointed out that Kiran nearly beat her.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Nandini praises her smashes?
qa.a: Kiran may feel respected and less crushed by the loss.

grounding: Shows over several days a teen who enjoys a win, thanks her coach and stays kind to the player who lost.

passage: You asked why I still keep this dented medal, beta. When I was fifteen, I won the state debate in Chandigarh. My knees shook through the whole final. My opponent was Gurleen, from a school across town, sharper than me on half the points. When they called my name I screamed like a child, I won't lie. Then I saw Gurleen's face. So I went over and said, "Your second argument nearly finished me." She laughed. Afterwards I thanked Mr Sandhu, our coach, who had made me practise in front of the mirror for weeks. Gurleen and I wrote letters for years. I, Jahnavi, learned that day you can be proud and still be kind. The medal got dented when I dropped it dancing.

qa.q: Where was the state debate held?
qa.a: In Chandigarh.

qa.q: What was young Jahnavi feeling when her name was called?
qa.a: Jahnavi was overjoyed and proud, screaming like a child, before noticing Gurleen's face.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Seeing Gurleen's face, Jahnavi went over and praised her argument instead of gloating.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt when Jahnavi came over?
qa.a: Gurleen likely felt respected and less hurt, which is why she laughed and they became friends.

grounding: Shows a teen who enjoys winning, thanks the coach and stays kind to the rival who lost.

passage: Gautam's quiz partner went down with fever the night before the inter-school final, so he faced the last round alone, in a hall where the fans had stopped working. Sweat ran down his collar. On the final question, the capital of Mongolia, he hit the buzzer and got it right. The small crowd erupted. Gautam grinned so widely his cheeks hurt. Then he crossed the stage to the other team, three boys from St. Paul's, and said, "That round on rivers, you were so fast, I was panicking." Outside he found Madhuri-ma'am, who had run extra practice every Saturday. "This is half yours," he said. That evening he didn't post about it; he just called his partner and went through every question.

qa.q: What was the final question?
qa.a: The capital of Mongolia.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when he won?
qa.a: He felt delighted and proud, grinning so widely his cheeks hurt.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that shows humility alongside pride?
qa.a: He praised the other team, thanked Madhuri-ma'am as half the reason and shared the win with his absent partner.

qa.q: How might the St. Paul's team feel when Gautam talks to them?
qa.a: They may feel respected and less disappointed, hearing that they had him worried.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who owns a win, thanks his coach and stays kind to those who lost, without needing an audience.

passage:
When the arbiter announced the result in the Hyderabad community hall, Farhan closed his eyes and let out a breath. First place, city under-16 chess. He'd lost to the same opponent last year.
Ishita, the girl he'd beaten in the final, was packing her pieces slowly, jaw tight. Farhan walked over first. "Your knight sacrifice in round two, I didn't see it coming. You nearly had me."
She managed a small smile. "Next year."
"Next year," he agreed.
He found Coach Reddy by the door and touched his feet. "Thank you, sir. The endgame drills worked."
His friends wanted him to post the trophy photo everywhere. Farhan shrugged. "Maybe later." On the bus home, he held the trophy on his lap and grinned at nothing.

qa.q: Who did Farhan beat in the final?
qa.a: Ishita.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel on the bus home?
qa.a: He felt quietly proud and happy, holding the trophy on his lap and grinning to himself.

qa.q: Which of Farhan's actions showed pride without contempt?
qa.a: Going first to Ishita to praise her knight sacrifice and thanking Coach Reddy for the drills.

qa.q: What was it like for Ishita when Farhan came over?
qa.a: She was disappointed, packing slowly with a tight jaw, but his specific praise let her smile and look ahead to next year.

grounding: Shows a teen who wins a competition, enjoys it, thanks his coach and stays kind to the player he beat, without needing an audience.
